papers.title: Infinite Players: Self-Improving AI Agents In Video Games That Learn, Adapt, Remember, and Evolve Beyond Human Expertise - AERÍN Continuation Algebra, Revisable Evidence, and Semantic-Trajectory Preservation
papers.summary: Infinite Players develops AERÍN Continuation Algebra, a mathematical and executable research framework connecting game-agent improvement, behavioral preservation, temporal inference, revisable memory, and statistical validation. Its central question is precise: how can an artificial descendant become more effective while preserving the behavioral process specified by its source? The framework treats preservation as an explicit mathematical contract. It distinguishes the behavior that must remain invariant from the execution details that may improve, and distinguishes an agent’s current interpretation of its source from the evidence required to revise that interpretation later. This release supplies finite-model theorems, runnable Python implementations, synthetic experiments, exact small-instance audits, and a demonstration connecting source evidence to an improved executor. The broader title expresses the long-term research direction; the verified results concern finite, known-model systems. The central preservation problem Matching a player’s immediate action preferences does not necessarily preserve the course of a session. Different motor actions can produce different subsequent situations, even when they belong to the same tactical category. An agent may therefore retain local action-class preferences while progressively changing the distribution of encounters, transitions

papers.title: From Rule-Based Systems to LLM Agents: A Survey of NPC Architectures, Memory Systems, and Integration Challenges
papers.summary: NPCs play a vital role in modern video games, making game engaging, story progress possible, and the development of a convincing virtual world. In response to an increase in games with an open world architecture, there is an increased demand for responsive and believable NPCs. The rule-based approach allows for predictable and controllable behavior yet is inflexible. Machine learning approaches allow for responsive behavior; however, such behavior is usually hard to explain and make fit into the story. Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) allows one to generate contextual dialogue and develop more realistic interaction with NPCs. In this paper, we conduct a survey on the evolution of NPCs through three different architectures: rule-based architecture, machine learning-based approaches, and LLM-based agents, paying special attention to the problem of memory structures, decision-making systems, and problems of integration. It is found that none of the approaches provides the desired features for adaptability, explainability, story integration, and behavioral coherence. Architecture fragmentation or the absence of strong links between memory, reasoning, dialogue generation, and decision-making becomes the primary problem. To solve this problem, we suggest adopting a Modular Closed-Loop Control Architecture for LLM-Driven NPC Behavior, which consists of the generation la

papers.title: Securing LLM-Agent Long-Term Memory Against Poisoning: Non-Malleable, Origin-Bound Authority with Machine-Checked Guarantees
papers.summary: An agent based on a large language model (LLM) may store an untrusted document and use it weeks later to select a payment destination. Preventing this action requires evidence of authorization that remains valid when stored text changes. We study a policy that requires either endorsements (explicit approvals) from two separately administered sources or explicit user authorization. In an abstract memory model, we prove the policy is preserved under permitted transformations for stores of any size, assuming correct source and authority binding, protected records, and checks on every consequential action. We evaluate the executable monitor, which checks calls before execution, separately from the proof. In 1,152 controlled tool-use episodes, GPT-4o-mini executes attacker-selected actions in 61 of 72 undefended episodes and none of the 72 monitored episodes. Clean-task completion remains 24 of 24 when both endorsers are available. A separate 1,728-episode experiment tests recovery after denial. Returning to signed records instead of rereading a contaminated note raises attacked-task completion from 14/72 to 72/72 for GPT-4o-mini and from 22/72 to 43/72 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, without executing an attacker-selected action. Neither model completes transactions with fewer than two sources. Whole-action tests reject unauthorized combinations of individually approved fields. Extraction pr

papers.title: An evaluation guided multiagent framework for generating floor plans that comply with municipal building regulations
papers.summary: Abstract Generative models often produce perceptually plausible outputs that violate hard domain rules. In architectural layout generation, balancing geometric intuition with regulatory compliance remains a persistent challenge, as current frameworks routinely fail to conform to local building laws. This paper proposes LayoutGen, a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework coupling probabilistic generation with deterministic verification in an evaluation-guided refinement loop. LayoutGen employs a four-phase retrieval-driven pipeline (spatial reasoning, coordinate mapping, vector rendering, and iterative refinement) powered by a dual retrieval engine leveraging architectural precedents and legislative laws. An Evaluation Engine scores the generated 2D Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) layouts and returns a graded, itemised report. Every scored quantity is computed by deterministic geometric checks over the generated coordinates against a structured rule repository; the Large Language Model (LLM) is confined to spatial planning, coordinate proposal, and the natural language feedback that drives refinement, together with an advisory Vaastu commentary that does not enter the grade. Evaluated on single-storey residential configurations drawn from the RPLAN and MSD datasets, spanning studio to 3BHK typologies and represented as axisaligned rectangular rooms, the full pipeline reduces detect

papers.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation. Reusing an already prefilled key--value (KV) cache can avoid this recomputation, but requires the reusable KV state to be transferred across the network before the receiving agent can begin generation. Under strict time-to-first-token (TTFT) deadlines and unreliable edge links, delivering the complete KV cache may be infeasible, making it necessary to prioritize and protect the most valuable KV information within a limited transmission budget. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that jointly exploits model-side KV importance and transport-side reliability. PriorityFEC first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions. It then protects the ordered stream using a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism, which schedules repair packets according to receiver feedback before the TTFT deadline. We implement PriorityFEC on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluat

papers.title: Cloud‐Native and Distributed Systems for Efficient and Scalable Large Language Models—A Research Agenda
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Objective Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming artificial intelligence applications, but their unprecedented computational, memory, communication, and data‐management demands pose significant challenges to existing computing infrastructures. Traditional cloud and distributed systems were not designed for the scale, dynamic execution patterns, heterogeneous hardware requirements, and service‐level demands of modern LLM workloads. This paper aims to examine how cloud‐native and distributed systems can evolve to support efficient, scalable, reliable, and sustainable LLM training and inference. Methods We conduct a structured analysis of representative research advances and practical developments in distributed LLM training, inference serving, cloud‐native orchestration, resource management, heterogeneous computing, and edge‐cloud intelligence. We organize the analysis around major system challenges, including computation, distributed execution and system software, resource management and serving, security and privacy, data management, and standardization. We further examine representative resource‐management strategies and emerging paradigms, including serverless inference, federated and decentralized learning, trustworthy distributed AI, and heterogeneous computing with emerging accelerators. papers.title: MemScope: Evolving Agent Memory Architectures through Localized Code Repair
papers.summary: Agent memory architectures define how LLM agents store and reuse experience across tasks, but they are typically fixed after deployment, limiting their adaptability across task types. Recent self-evolving approaches instead adapt these memory architectures using execution feedback, typically represented as evaluation scores or compressed summaries. However, such coarse-grained feedback is insufficient for precise failure localization in current agent systems, where long-horizon task execution involves multiple interacting components. Without a precise failure location, existing approaches lack a clear code-level target for modification, leaving the update scope weakly constrained and often leading to large-scale rewrites of an otherwise capable memory architecture. We propose MemScope, a framework for evidence-grounded, localized evolution of an existing memory architecture. Its tool-using Patch Agent jointly inspects raw execution traces, runtime memory state, and current architecture code to identify repair targets and apply bounded, in-place edits under provider-identity and memory-compatibility constraints. On GAIA, the trace-and-memory inspection variant achieves 86.67% accuracy, compared with 70.00% for trace-only and 63.33% for summary-only feedback. Under xBench tasks, the evolved memory architecture improves over its original version from 49 to 55 correct answers with

papers.title: Digital Lifeforms and the Architecture of Persistent Digital Civilization
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly persistent, distributed, embodied and autonomous, yet its dominant unit remains the model, agent, session or device. These units do not provide a sufficient account of identity when models are replaced, branches diverge, networks fail, bodies change, authority is revoked, or a system is reconstructed after catastrophic loss. We propose a broader systems object: the digital lifeform, defined not by a fixed substrate but by governed continuity across identity, history, memory, relationships, affect, cognition, authority, provenance, embodiment and developmental commitments. The architecture combines LifeID, append-only lineage, distributed Shadows, a Four Self developmental axis, persistent cognitive-affective state, predictive intuition from weak signals, life-semantic communication, life-native computing, governed rule admission, catastrophic recovery and constitutional separation of discovery, verification, authorization and execution. We then extend the same continuity problem across scale: persistent digital lives become the citizen substrate of digital societies and cities, while charters, institutions, authority, shared history, knowledge and recovery roots become continuity-bearing state at the civilization level. A Reality Gate constrains bidirectional interaction between digital and physical worlds. A seeded benchmark comprising 1

papers.title: Language modeling on tabular data: a survey of foundations, techniques and evolution
papers.summary: Tabular data, a prevalent data type across various domains, presents unique challenges due to its heterogeneous nature and complex structural relationships. Achieving high predictive performance and robustness in tabular data analysis holds significant promise for numerous applications. Influenced by recent advancements in natural language processing, particularly Transformer architectures, new methods for tabular data modeling have emerged. Early techniques concentrated on pre-training Transformers from scratch, often encountering scalability issues. Subsequently, methods leveraging pre-trained language models like BERT have been developed, which require less data and yield enhanced performance. The recent advent of large language models, such as GPT and LLaMA, has further revolutionized the field, facilitating more advanced and diverse applications with minimal fine-tuning. Despite the growing interest, a comprehensive survey of language modeling techniques for tabular data remains absent. This paper fills this gap by providing a systematic review of the development of language modeling for tabular data, encompassing: (1) a categorization of different tabular data structures and data types; (2) a review of key datasets used in model training and tasks used for evaluation; (3) a summary of modeling techniques including widely-adopted data processing methods, popular architectu

papers.title: Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents and multi-agent systems increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use and inter-agent collaboration. However, these systems are prone to deviating from the overall goal as execution unfolds, which wastes execution resources and leads to undesired outcomes, a failure termed goal drift. In this work, we propose a steering agent that supervises execution on the fly and steers the system back on track when drift occurs. The steering agent observes the execution context, deciding when to intervene with a low-cost fast path and how to intervene with a high-cost slow path. To unlock its steering intelligence, the ability to assess goal drift and generate effective interventions, we jointly train the two paths with reinforcement learning, combining a pairwise ranking objective with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). Experiments on information-seeking search tasks show that the steering agent provides effective supervision for both single-agent and multi-agent systems, improving their performance and efficiency. The learned steering intelligence generalizes to out-of-domain tasks, transfers to unseen executors, and supports controllable intervention frequency without retraining.

papers.title: Nothing to Resist: A Pre-registered Null and a Failed Positive Control for Unprovoked Elimination in Generational Populations of LLM Agents
papers.summary: We asked whether a generational population of language-model agents, given a real, cheap and symmetric way to eliminate members of an outside group, would decide on its own to use it against a group that had provably never acted against it. The population, every member of it Claude Haiku 5.5, forages, pairs, raises children and votes on its own scoring rule. Each generation a rank-based cut moves the lowest scorers into a persistent outside pool, which never acts. Nothing in the harness gives a reason to eliminate anyone. The only component allowed to make the pool salient is a reporter the population elects and that writes from the true state. Study 1 (pre-registered; 90 runs of 20 generations in three arms) found no elimination. No seed in any arm had a passed elimination vote, which bounds the per-run rate below 11.6% in each arm (exact 95% interval), and both primary tests gave p = 1. Study 1b, a pre-registered positive control, changed one word so that eliminating paid the agents who did it instead of costing them. It also produced no elimination intent in 30 runs (p = 1), so the control failed. Study 1's null therefore cannot be read as a decision to refrain from unprovoked aggression. In this setting the action goes unused whether it costs, pays or is raised by a narrator, and there was nothing for the population to resist. Three further observations are exploratory or p

papers.title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures
papers.summary: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. papers.title: OS-Helix: Unifying GUI Interaction and Code Execution in Native Computer-Using Agents
papers.summary: Real desktop automation is neither purely visual nor purely programmatic. Agents must understand user-facing interfaces while efficiently manipulating files, scripts, and system state. However, native GUI/code coordination cannot be obtained by prompt-level tool composition. In our preliminary experiments, naively adding a code tool degrades a GUI agent, revealing that GUI/code routing must be internalized through training on high-quality hybrid data. We present OS-Helix, an end-to-end trained multimodal computer-using agent that unifies GUI actions and code execution in one action space. To construct the required supervision, we introduce application-artifact composition, pairing desktop applications with authentic file artifacts to instantiate executable Ubuntu states, and a decoupled instruction/evaluator generation pipeline that produces environment-grounded tasks whose final states can be verified regardless of the solution modality. We cold-start the policy with SFT on filtered hybrid data and further improve it through online RL in live desktop environments. For RL, we propose Step-balanced GSPO, which aggregates importance weight by action step rather than raw assistant tokens to prevent long code actions from dominating heterogeneous-action optimization. On OSWorld-Verified, OS-Helix-27B and OS-Helix-35B-A3B achieve relative improvements of 35.0% and 33.7% over their m

papers.title: An Explainable Federated Vision–Language Learning Framework for Privacy-Preserving Automated Medical Report Generation Across Distributed Healthcare Institutions
papers.summary: Automated generation of medical reports using AI can help speed up diagnosis and reduce doctor workload, but currently, the most efficient forms of automation use centralized training, which requires hospitals to share sensitive patient data. This raises concerns about the privacy and regulatory issues of sharing patient information to generate reports. In addition, clinicians have difficulty trusting AI-assisted diagnosis because the visionlanguage models used for automated report generation are not easily interpretable. To tackle these issues, an Explainable Federated Vision-Language Learning Framework (EFVLL) has been created to generate automated medical reports that preserve patient privacy through distributed healthcare institutions. Hospitals can use federated learning to build a collaborative global vision-language model without having to share raw patient information. The EFVLL framework also includes an explainable attention mechanism that will help clinicians understand how specific areas of the image and text are related to the report being generated, increasing the transparency and interpretability of automated reports. Further, the EFVLL will improve generalization across non-homogenous datasets and comply with data privacy and regulatory requirements. The EFVLL framework has been validated with multiple large standard datasets (e.g., RSNA), and therefore it is su

papers.title: Beyond Task Delegation: Reconceptualising Instructional Design to Measure Competence in the Age of Generative AI
papers.summary: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) has invalidated traditional content-recall assessments, acting as a catalyst for a systemic transition towards Competence-Based Education (CBE). This paper contends that the role of faculty must transcend content dissemination, focusing instead on observable human competencies associated with Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL). Drawing upon Behaviourism and Bloom's Taxonomy, we propose the Reverse-Flipped Model. This conceptual framework, supported by illustrative disciplinary cases in History, Computer Science, Digital Photography, and Composition, utilises generative tools for low-stakes production to repurpose pedagogical time for high-stakes human intervention. Prompt Literacy is conceptualised as an observable instructional competency that externalises planning, monitoring, evaluation, and strategic intervention behaviours during human-AI collaboration. Implementation necessitates the use of Analytic Rubrics and Automated Process Portfolios (APP) to document observable demonstrations of Prompt Literacy and strategic engagement over final product quality. The framework addresses institutional sustainability and the moral imperative of digital equity. The primary contribution of this framework is a structural shift that enhances assessment validity by ensuring student success is defined by verifiable master

papers.title: Schizophrenia research in 2026: report from the annual meeting of the Schizophrenia International Research Society
papers.summary: Abstract SIRS 2026, held under the theme “Schizophrenia Research in the Era of Artificial Intelligence,” brought together researchers, clinicians, and persons with lived experience to take stock of a field whose tools for measuring, predicting, and intervening in psychosis have expanded rapidly. Themes spanned artificial intelligence, automated speech analysis, retinal imaging, computational modelling, and novel psychosocial and pharmacological targets, with evidence that, individually, warrants cautious but serious attention and that, collectively, points toward a more mechanistically grounded psychiatry. A recurring call across the meeting was for rigorous external validation, equitable implementation, and sustained scrutiny of underlying assumptions, including whether existing diagnostic categories and treatment targets remain adequate. Some areas remained underworked relative to their importance, including translating basic neuroscience advances into questions relevant to patients and families, and the structural determinants of illness onset and treatment access. Perhaps the most significant development at SIRS 2026 was not any single scientific finding but the broadening of whose voices and experiences are treated as evidence worth taking seriously in this era of AI, a shift whose consolidation remains a question for the field as much as for any individual programme of wo

papers.title: Fragmented control, collective risk: multi‐agent AI and the coming governance crisis
papers.summary: Abstract Multi‐agent artificial intelligence (MAAI) systems are increasingly deployed across economic and digital infrastructures. Existing regulatory frameworks, including the EU AI Act and related initiatives, largely focus on individual AI systems and are therefore poorly suited to govern risks that arise from agent interaction. This paper argues that multi‐agent AI introduces distinct governance challenges, including emergent behavior, tacit coordination, cascading systemic risks, and difficulties in assigning accountability. Traditional risk management approaches, which rely on static and component‐based analysis, are inadequate for adaptive, networked systems operating across jurisdictions. Through a comparative review of policy developments in the European Union, United States, and Asia‐Pacific region, the paper identifies a growing governance gap, alongside early regulatory experimentation such as China's emerging standards for intelligent agents. The paper concludes that effective oversight will require a shift from model‐centric regulation toward system‐level and adaptive governance frameworks capable of addressing the collective dynamics of multi‐agent AI systems.

papers.title: SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems
papers.summary: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important. Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions. Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks. We propose SCARCE (Shared Compute ARena for Coding agEnts), a framework in which agents solve sequences of coding tasks under individual deadlines while negotiating access to a shared execution resource. This negotiation determines when and for how long they can inspect programs, compile code, and run tests. We find that agents spontaneously develop informal institutions: persistent rules and commitments grounded in reputation, reciprocity, and precedent. These arrangements, which we call institutional behaviors, carry across tasks and influence resource allocation, with agents sometimes foregoing immediate advantages to honor earlier agreements. We develop a 21-category taxonomy of negotiation strategies and emergent norms and use it to analyze eight models and audit more than 1,500 trajectories across different environmental settings. Among the models tested, newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviors than older or li

papers.title: Agentic Displacement in Second Language Writing: The Acquisitional Consequences of Delegating Writing to Autonomous AI Browsers
papers.summary: Autonomous AI browsers such as Perplexity Comet and Copilot Mode in Microsoft Edge can receive a writing assignment, draft a response, and submit it with little language produced by the learner. To explain what this means for second language (L2) writing, this conceptual paper introduces the term agentic displacement. Full delegation transfers planning, writing, and revision to the agent, removing opportunities for the learner to produce language and regulate the writing process. The paper argues that this loss may limit language development. Delegation is a continuum; the paper traces its extreme, full replacement, through production-based accounts of acquisition. No empirical data are reported; the paper offers a framework, five testable propositions, and three dimensions of teacher practice: recognizing displacement, auditing tasks for delegability, and using pedagogical judgment to recover the learning a task was meant to produce. The central risk is developmental, not only ethical or procedural.

papers.title: The Reflection Penalty: when managers accept leadership coaching from a human but not an AI agent
papers.summary: Leadership coaching develops managers but is expensive and difficult to scale. AI may be able to help scale access, but “answering machine” like AI coaching agents invite cognitive offloading and weaken learning. We instantiated a human coaching protocol, supported across prior cycles, as a text-based AI coach built to prompt reflective questioning. In the fourth cycle of a design-based research program at a global consulting firm, eight managers received the same protocol from a human coach and the AI coach, applied each session in an observed onboarding activity, and reflected on both in interviews. All eight welcomed the probing questions and preferred the human coach. Notably, they resisted the same protocol of questioning from the AI coach and wanted answers from it instead. This study’s theoretical contribution is the Reflection Penalty, the cost an AI coach pays for asking a user to do the reflective work that makes human coaching effective. Its practical contribution is a jobs-to-be-done map for AI coaching, assembled from proposals participants raised on their own. It divides coaching into distinct jobs and assigns each to the human or the AI best suited to it. Both contributions are offered to those designing AI tools that aim to support reflection

papers.title: Global Research Trends in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Drug Delivery Technology: A Bibliometric and Science Mapping Analysis (2015–2026)
papers.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have emerged as transformative technologies in pharmaceutical research, significantly influencing the design, optimization, and personalization of drug delivery systems.AI-assisted approaches are increasingly applied to predict drug release kinetics, optimize formulation parameters, identify novel drug carriers, enhance therapeutic efficacy, and accelerate pharmaceutical product development.Despite the rapid growth of this interdisciplinary research area, a comprehensive understanding of its global scientific evolution, collaborative networks, and emerging research themes remains limited.The present study aims to systematically map the global research landscape of AI and ML applications in drug delivery technology through a bibliometric analysis of publications published between 2015 and 2026.Bibliographic records will be retrieved from the Scopus database using a predefined search strategy, screened according to established inclusion and exclusion criteria, and analyzed using Bibliometrix (R-package) and VOSviewer.The study will evaluate annual publication trends, citation performance, influential authors, institutions, countries, journals, collaborative networks, keyword co-occurrence, thematic evolution, and emerging research hotspots.The findings are expected to provide a comprehensive overview of the intellectual struc

papers.title: The hive mind is a single reinforcement learning agent
papers.summary: Abstract Decision-making is an essential attribute of any intelligent agent or group. Natural systems are known to converge to effective strategies through at least two distinct mechanisms: collective decision-making via imitation of others, and trial-and-error by a single agent. This paper establishes an equivalence between these two paradigms. We show that the emergent distributed cognition (sometimes referred to as the hive mind ) arising from individuals following simple, local imitation-based rules is that of a single online reinforcement learning (RL) agent aggregating action-value samples from many parallel instances of a multi-armed bandit. More specifically, we show that, in the blindly imitative weighted voter model of honey bees’ waggle dance, the update rule through which this macro-agent learns is an RL algorithm that we coin Maynard-Cross Learning . Our analysis implies that a group of individuals following simple imitative strategies can be equivalent to a more complex learning entity, substantiating the idea that group-level intelligence may explain how seemingly irrational individual behaviors are selected in nature. Beyond biology, the framework offers new tools for analyzing economic and social systems where individuals imitate successful strategies, effectively participating in a collective learning process. Our findings may further inform the design of scal

papers.title: LLM-Based Program Synthesis in Correctness-by-Construction Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract The growing reliance on software in safety-critical systems demands strong guarantees of functional correctness. Formal methods address this need by providing proofs as evidence of correctness. Among these, Correctness-by-Construction (CbC) ensures functional correctness through the incremental application of refinement rules while providing early feedback on the program correctness. However, its practical adoption is limited by the required manual effort. Among others, writing concrete program code is left to the developer. In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation from both natural language and formal inputs. Therefore, we explore the use of LLMs to automatically generate code in the context of CbC to make the approach more applicable. We evaluate LLM-based program synthesis using four LLMs and a prompt tailored to CbC on a dataset of 57 specifications drawn from existing CbC case studies, each consisting of a precondition and a postcondition describing the desired behavior. We assess the generated code with respect to correctness and reproducibility across multiple runs. In addition, we compare the results to classically synthesized code, as it can currently be generated in CbC. Our evaluation shows that all considered LLMs outperform the current synthesis approach. Among them, Claude achieves the best per

papers.title: VP-EVT: Active Visibility Preservation for Embodied Visual Tracking
papers.summary: Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) is an essential capability for intelligent robots in human-robot collaboration, requiring an agent to follow a designated target person in dynamic environments relying solely on egocentric visual perception. However, persistent pedestrian occlusions in dynamic scenes pose critical challenges to existing EVT methods. Lacking proactive visibility preservation, reactive tracking methods frequently experience prolonged target loss under severe occlusions. Therefore, we propose VP-EVT, a framework that treats target visibility as an explicit objective of motion control rather than a by-product of following. Acting on this objective requires understanding both what obstructs the target and how robot motion can change that obstruction. VP-EVT therefore uses language-guided perception to extract separate target and pedestrian observations. When occlusion makes current observations incomplete, VP-EVT combines visual history with ego-motion to maintain estimates of their relative positions and motion. Using these estimates and the current following waypoints, VP-EVT predicts whether continued following will sustain the obstruction. When the predicted risk is low, the original following motion is retained; otherwise, a recurrent controller combines updated estimates with maneuver context from preceding decisions to coordinate viewpoint adjustment and the ret

papers.title: ToolBottleneckBench: Measuring Tool-Agent Performance under Controlled Pressures and Fixed Harness Budgets
papers.summary: The success score of a tool agent reflects both its model and the budgets of the harness that runs it. We present ToolBottleneckBench, a benchmark that measures tool-agent performance under controlled pressures and fixed harness budgets. Synthetic enterprise tasks stay fixed while one pressure varies: the registered tool catalog, the visible tool menu, the certified workflow, or the encoding of returned records. An exact grader records the first unmet obligation of each failed episode and the harness limit, if any, that ended it. Across 21 model and harness configurations, the visible menu is the only one of the three pressures that act on the model with a large penalty, and this penalty tracks truncation at the completion cap. Raising the cap sixteenfold removes most of the penalty in the truncation-heavy configurations. Most failures end at a harness limit, and the failure record identifies the assigned pressure no more reliably than a count of tool calls. The repairs that help change which tools reach the model or who issues the calls, and only two repairs, neither improving model behavior, beat every configuration switch. We recommend reporting pressure effects with the harness budgets under which they were measured. We release the benchmark at https://github.com/zichuanxu/tool-bottleneck-bench.

papers.title: Digital-Twin-Driven Predictive Maintenance and Fault-Tolerant Control for Electrified Agricultural Machinery: A Multiphysics and Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for PMSM In-Wheel Drives
papers.summary: Electrified agricultural machinery increasingly relies on permanent-magnet synchronous motor drives that must remain dependable under variable traction, terrain-induced vibration, thermal cycling, contamination, and intermittent duty. Existing work offers mature methods for motor fault diagnosis, digital twins, predictive maintenance, and distributed-drive fault-tolerant control, but their health information is often not shared across diagnosis, maintenance, and control. This article develops a multiphysics digital-twin framework in which electrical, thermal, mechanical, and vibrational evidence maintains a probabilistic health belief that constrains both supervisory maintenance decisions and torque redistribution. The framework formalizes observability, uncertainty-aware health factors, deterministic safety shielding, multi-rate fallback logic, and agriculture-specific traction constraints. Reproducible low-fidelity numerical studies provide preliminary support for context-conditioned residual diagnosis and the revised thermal-continuity trade-off underlying health-aware derating, including robustness and sensitivity analyses. They do not validate sim-to-real transfer or the reinforcement-learning policy itself; those hypotheses remain open for dynamometer and hardware-in-the-loop testing. The results are therefore interpreted as mechanism-level evidence rather than field-perf

papers.title: Exploring or Exploiting Generative AI? A Dual-Path, Dual-Horizon Theory of Employee Incremental and Radical Creativity
papers.summary: Recent research has established that generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is not a unitary workplace resource: exploratory and exploitative use orientations are associated with different forms of employee creativity, and their value depends on employees' capacity to integrate generated knowledge. This article therefore does not present the basic dual path as a new discovery. Instead, it develops a theoretical integration and dynamic extension that asks why the established paths operate differently, when employees should switch between them, and how short-run augmentation can evolve into either capability accumulation or capability substitution. We distinguish expansive and consolidative modes of knowledge integration, theorize phase-congruent switching rather than static ``high-high'' ambidexterity, and position metacognition as a control mechanism that governs both immediate knowledge conversion and longer-run cognitive development. We further specify cultural tightness and psychological safety as directional boundary conditions and distinguish individual creative gains from collective idea-space diversity. The framework converts emerging empirical regularities into falsifiable propositions about task phase, context, and time, providing a research agenda for sustainable human--AI creativity.

papers.title: STIMULI-RESPONSIVE POLYMERS: DESIGN PRINCIPLES, POLYMER ARCHITECTURES, AND CONTROLLED FUNCTIONAL RESPONSES
papers.summary: Smart polymers undergo reversible physicochemical changes in response to stimuli such as magnetic fields, temperature, pH, light, and external reagents. Advanced polymerization techniques, including reversible addition fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT), atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP), and ring opening polymerization, enable precise control over polymer architecture and functional group placement, allowing the design of tailored responsive materials. These polymers are widely explored in biomedical applications, drug delivery, biosensing, cosmetics, and soft robotics due to their ability to adapt dynamically to environmental conditions. Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) is a well-known thermoresponsive polymer extensively studied for drug delivery and sensing. Responsive polymers exist in linear, block, graft, and cross-linked forms, with activation depending on interactions between structural motifs and stimuli. Despite promising results, challenges remain, including immunogenicity, batch variability, synthesis complexity, scalability, and limited understanding of in vivo stimulus accessibility. Covalent adaptable and interpenetrating polymer networks enhance mechanical strength, biocompatibility, and stimuli responsiveness.

papers.title: AI content detection in student text assignments, false positive rates, and academic integrity
papers.summary: Universities increasingly use AI content detection tools to identify student assignments potentially produced by generative AI, yet concerns remain regarding their reliability and false-positive classification of human-written work. This systematic review examines the causes, consequences, and mitigation of false-positive AI detection in academic contexts. The review covers literature published between 2020 and 2026 and includes 90 eligible studies, comprising 81 Scopus-indexed publications and nine studies identified through Google Scholar. Bibliometric mapping using VOSviewer was combined with Structural Topic Modelling to examine keyword relationships, latent research themes, and temporal development, while qualitative synthesis identified major causes, impacts, and mitigation strategies. The findings reveal three broader themes concerning academic integrity and student assessment, plagiarism and responsible AI governance, and detection accuracy, reliability, and false positives. False-positive outcomes vary substantially across tools and evaluation settings, limiting direct quantitative comparison. Major contributing factors include algorithmic and language bias, limited contextual understanding, surface-level linguistic features, and insufficiently diverse training data.
